newsitem.title: UK: Precious metal prices up on S.African strike.
newsitem.headline: Precious metal prices up on S.African strike.

text.p: Prices of the platinum group metals (PGMs) surged to fresh high levels on Wedensday on news of an unofficial strike at a major mine in South Africa.
Palladium was fixed at its highest level since the official fixings began in 1989 of $188.00, up from $177.50 on Tuesday.
Platinum's fix of $404.50 was its highest since August 1, 1996 and up from $398.00 previously.
"The prices have more to do with the very tight physical position of the markets rather than Rustenburg," one dealer said referring to the scramble by dealers to buy or borrow either metal.
Their scarcity results from Russia the largest palladium exporter and second biggest platinum supplier after South Africa failing to export this year due to administrative problems.

It has been reflected in the cost of borrowing the metals between dealers soaring from a normal two-three percent for a month to 41 percent for palladium and 17 percent for its sister metal in the past week, dealers said.
"The price is not going to come back down dramatically while the market is this tight," a platinum dealer said.
Russia is expected to begin 1997 PGM exports during early June.
The metals are used in electronics and autocatalysts for cleaning up car exhaust gases. Platinum is also used for jewellery and palladium for dental alloys.
Rustenburg is the world's largest platinum mine. Its production of over 1.2 million ounces of platinum a year represents about 25 percent of world supply.
Last year about 100,000 ounces of production was lost through a three-week unofficial strike that sent prices soaring.
Gold was fixed just $1.05 ahead of Tuesday at $344.70.
Dealers said business was cautious as they watched for any comments on Germany's plans to revalue its gold reserves following Wednesday's meeting of the Bundesbank Council.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel shocked the market earlier this month when he announced Germany would revalue its gold reserves closer to market prices to help the country meet budgetary targets ahead of the 1999 European Monetary Union.
Germany has traditionally opposed any mobilisation of gold reserves, seeing them as a key anti-inflation weapon.
The market feared this could mean Germany's near 3,000 tonnes of gold becoming active in the market.
Silver was largely ignored and was marked up only two cents from Tuesday's close to $4.76/$4.78.
